newsitem.title: BELGIUM: 500,000 T U.S maize at risk in EU gene row-sources.
newsitem.headline: 500,000 T U.S maize at risk in EU gene row-sources.

text.p: Some 500,000 tonnes of Spanish preferential imports of U.S. maize for 1996 could be blocked if the European Union decides to ban genetically-modified maize, EU sources estimated.
They said that Spain could switch to Argentine maize, although supplies would only be available in a few months time.

A ban on gene-modified maize would effectively block all shipments from the U.S., where the grain is not separated into conventional and transgenic supplies. The U.S. says it is impossible to do this without incurring heavy additional costs.
The European Commission is due on December 18 to decide whether to allow gene-modified maize, developed by Swiss company Ciba-Geigy AG and grown in the United States, on to the EU market.

European consumer and environmental groups want to ban the maize, which has been engineered to resist the corn borer pest and certain weedkillers, because they believe it poses a public and animal health risk.

Madrid normally imports two million tonnes of maize at a reduced tariff under a long-standing agreement to compensate U.S. and other maize exporters for losses after Spain joined the EU in 1985. Traditionally the maize is shipped from the U.S.
Around 1.5 million tonnes has already been imported under the 1996 quota either as maize grain or by-products, such as corn gluten feed, a source estimated.
EU imports of maize have fallen sharply this season following a 15 percent surge in production compared with the drought-affected 1995/96 harvest.
The EU imported only 218,000 tonnes between July 1 and December 3, 1996, down from 1.05 million tonnes in the same period last year.

Only importers with urgent or special needs -- such as breakfast cereals -- have been importing maize as the current import tariff on trans-Atlantic shipments has climbed to nearly 82 Ecus a tonne, the source added.
